raw_case_text:
A fifty-year-old female patient presented to us 45 days after an uneventful manual small incision cataract surgery. The patient was from a farming background and otherwise she did not have any health issues and she was not a diabetic. She gave history of mild pain, redness, and blurred vision in the operated eye (left eye) for five days. On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was 6/6 and in the left eye hand movements were perceived close to face. On slit lamp examination, left eye had corneal epithelial edema and fluffy white cotton ball-like exudates in the anterior chamber and the intraocular lens was surrounded by the same exudates in the capsular bag (Figure 1). Intraocular pressure was normal. Ultrasound of the eye showed fine vitreous opacities of low reflectivity with flat retina (Figure 2).
Because of delayed onset and the type of exudates in the anterior chamber, fungal endophthalmitis was a strong suspicion. Pars plana vitrectomy with anterior chamber wash was done and intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were given. Direct microscopic examination of vitreous and anterior chamber fluid showed Gram-positive thin long beaded branching filaments and acid fast thin long filaments in modified acid fast staining (Kinyoun stain) (Figure 3). On blood agar dry, raised, chalky white colonies were seen after 2 days of incubation (Figure 4). The colonies were further identified as Nocardia asteroids based on colony morphology and biochemical reactions. The isolate was susceptible to amikacin, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, and co-trimoxazole.
Depending on the sensitivity report, intravitreal amikacin (200 mug/0.1 mL) was given. The dose of intravitreal amikacin was halved because it was a vitrectomised eye. Topical gatifloxacin and gentamicin eye drops were continued. Systemically, tablet co-trimoxazole was started and given for 6 weeks. Two weeks later, vision had improved to counting fingers at one meter. Anterior segment was quiet, mildly hazy vitreous and the macula was pale and cloudy looking with multiple intraretinal hemorrhages (Figure 5). Amikacin induced macular infarction was suspected. Fluorescein angiography showed multiple capillary nonperfusion areas (Figure 6). The OCT showed increased macular thickness (central foveal thickness 342 mum), hyperreflectivity of inner retinal layers corresponding to areas of retinal edema (Figure 7).
To treat this ischemia and inflammation induced macular edema, intravitreal steroids could not be used in the backdrop of endophthalmitis. Intravitreal Bevacizumab was used for its anti-inflammatory properties. The vision improved to counting fingers at 2 meters and the macular edema subsided (Figure 8). On OCT, the macular thickness had decreased but the differentiation of different retinal layers was not evident and foveal centre showed hyper dense and adherent RPE and retinal layers (Figure 9). After follow-up of more than three months now, the condition of the eye is stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old female farmer presented 45 days after uneventful left cataract surgery with a 5-day history of mild left eye pain, redness, and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Forty-five days after undergoing an uneventful manual small-incision cataract surgery in the left eye, the patient developed mild ocular pain, redness, and decreased vision over 5 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uneventful left manual small-incision cataract surgery 45 days prior; farming background; non-diabetic with no other systemic comorbidities.

objective.physical_examination: Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and hand movements close to the face in the left eye; intraocular pressure was normal. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed corneal epithelial edema and fluffy white cotton-ball-like exudates in the anterior chamber and surrounding the intraocular lens within the capsular bag.
objective.routine_investigations: B-scan ocular ultrasound of the left eye showed fine low-reflectivity vitreous opacities with an attached flat retina.
objective.advanced_workup: Pars plana vitrectomy and anterior chamber washout were performed. Antibiotic susceptibility testing of the intraocular isolate showed susceptibility to amikacin, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, and co-trimoxazole. Two weeks after intravitreal amikacin, funduscopy showed a pale, cloudy macula with multiple intraretinal hemorrhages; fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple areas of capillary nonperfusion; and macular OCT showed retinal edema with central foveal thickness of 342 um and inner retinal hyperreflectivity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by Nocardia asteroides complicated by amikacin-induced macular infarction was confirmed: direct microscopy of vitreous and anterior chamber fluid demonstrated Gram-positive thin beaded branching filaments that were partially acid-fast on modified Kinyoun stain, and blood agar culture grew dry, raised, chalky-white colonies after 2 days identified as Nocardia asteroides. Following initial intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole, she received half-dose intravitreal amikacin (200 ug/0.1 mL in a vitrectomized eye), topical gatifloxacin and gentamicin drops, and oral co-trimoxazole for 6 weeks. Amikacin-induced macular ischemia/edema was subsequently treated with intravitreal bevacizumab, resolving the macular edema and stabilizing visual acuity at counting fingers at 2 meters at >3-month follow-up.
